entities.name: Miklós Bercsényi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Count Miklós Bercsényi (1665–1725) emerged as a pivotal figure in early 18th-century Hungarian history, serving as chief general and principal diplomat for Francis II Rákóczi during the 1703–1711 War of Independence against Habsburg rule. Born into a prominent aristocratic family with extensive landholdings in Upper Hungary (modern-day Slovakia), Bercsényi's commitment to Hungarian sovereignty and his strategic acumen positioned him as the rebellion's second-in-command, shaping its military campaigns and foreign policy. His efforts were central to challenging the centralized authority of the Habsburg Monarchy and advocating for Hungarian constitutional rights within the broader context of European power struggles, particularly involving France and the Ottoman Empire.

Bercsényi played a dual role as both military commander and lead diplomat throughout the eight-year conflict. After joining Rákóczi in exile and returning to Hungary to ignite the uprising in 1703, he organized the Kuruc forces, leading several key engagements. His military contributions included the Siege of Érsekújvár (1703) and the Battle of Zsibó (1705), though the latter resulted in a significant defeat. On the diplomatic front, Bercsényi engaged in extensive negotiations with Louis XIV's France, securing crucial financial and military support, and later with Russia under Peter the Great, seeking a new alliance. He was instrumental in drafting the Act of Exiled Estates (1707), which formally dethroned the Habsburgs, and participated in the ultimately failed peace talks at Kassa and Trencsén.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Miklós Bercsényi's military and diplomatic leadership as second-in-command of Rákóczi's War of Independence significantly challenged Habsburg authority in Hungary for nearly a decade (1703-1711), inspiring future Hungarian nationalist movements and influencing the Habsburgs' later policy towards their Hungarian territories.
